title: Why Your Friend's 'Business Opportunity' Loses Money (MLMs)

spine.goal: Dave wants an easy side income from his neighbor Bob's 'business opportunity' (Bob says the $499 starter kit 'pays for itself in a month').
spine.stakes: Six months in he has spent $1,649 (kit $499 + autoship $900 + rally $250), sold only $240, has 40 boxes of shakes in the garage, and is about to recruit his own Grandma.
spine.central_question: If almost everybody in these businesses loses money, where does all that money go?
spine.loop_big: The one sentence that got Dave most of his money back (paid in the last minute: the 90% inventory buyback request, $945 back, damage $1,649 -> $464).
spine.loop_mid: Pause-and-guess (~30%): out of ~108,000 US distributors of one of the biggest MLMs, how many earn anything in a typical month? Paid ~60 s later: about 47,000, fewer than half (Herbalife's own 2025 statement).
spine.villain: The pay plan itself (revealed ~50%): Dave's monthly autoship flows UP the line to the company and the few at the top; Bob earned on Dave's orders, so Dave was Bob's customer, not his partner. Bob is a victim too.
spine.low_point: ~75%: Dave finds he has typed 'Hey hun! Exciting opportunity' to Grandma - he has become Bob - while $1,649 down with 40 boxes in the garage; Bob admits he is losing money too.
spine.win: Dave fights back (education, not advice): cancels autoship in writing, uses the DSA code's 90% buyback on $1,050 of unopened products (+$945), and for next time asks for the income disclosure + the FTC's two questions. Final damage $464 instead of $1,649.

sources: Story note: Dave, Bob, 'Bob's company', the miracle shakes and all of Dave's personal amounts ($499 kit, $150/month autoship, $250 rally, $240 sold, $1,050 unopened, $945 back, $464 final) are an illustrative dramatization, not a real company or real case.

AARP Foundation, 'Multilevel Marketing: The Research, Risks and Rewards' survey (released Oct 9, 2018; 1,016 respondents incl. 601 current/former MLM participants), via AARP Foundation press release (PR Newswire) and AARP.org: 47% of participants lost money, 27% broke even (73% total 'lose money or make no money'); only 25% made a profit and 53% of those made less than $5,000; 34% were recruited by friends and 12% by family; 41% said the company misled them about their chances of financial success; 39% stopped because pitching to friends and family felt uncomfortable; two-thirds would not join the same MLM again.

Herbalife, 'U.S. Statement of Typical Distributor Earnings 2025' (published June 2026, herbalife.com): about 107,769 U.S. Distributors ordered products for resale in 2025; in a typical month about 47,000 earned money (so fewer than half); first-year distributors who earned in a typical month: 50% earned more than $166 in a month; all other distributors: top 1% (about 410) earned more than $21,893 in a month; tenure of the top 1% typically 5-12 years; all figures before expenses.

FTC press release, July 15, 2016, 'Herbalife Will Restructure Its Multi-level Marketing Operations and Pay $200 Million For Consumer Redress to Settle FTC Charges': FTC alleged the overwhelming majority of distributors earn little or no money; settlement requires at least two-thirds of rewards paid to distributors be based on retail sales; independent compliance auditor for seven years.
FTC press release, Jan 10, 2017, 'FTC Sends Checks to Nearly 350,000 Victims of Herbalife's Multi-Level Marketing Scheme'.

FTC Consumer Advice, 'Multi-Level Marketing Businesses and Pyramid Schemes' (updated July 2022): 'Most people who join legitimate MLMs make little or no money. Some of them lose money.' Legit MLM = pay based on sales to retail customers; pyramid scheme = pay mainly from recruiting; warning sign: distributors buying more inventory than they can sell to stay active or qualify for bonuses; questions to ask: annual earnings after expenses, share of income from retail sales vs recruiting.

FTC, 'Business Guidance Concerning Multi-Level Marketing' (Jan 2018): compensation should be based on actual retail sales to real customers, not on recruiting or on participants' own purchases made to qualify for rewards.

Direct Selling Association, Code of Ethics (dsa.org): member companies agree to repurchase marketable inventory, sales aids and kits bought within 12 months at not less than 90 percent of the salesperson's original net cost (less set-offs); member companies may not require or encourage inventory purchases that unreasonably exceed what can be resold.

Direct Selling Education Foundation / DSA, '2026 Growth & Outlook Study' (2025 data, reported Aug 2026): $34.2 billion in U.S. direct-selling retail sales, 5.2 million direct sellers, 4.8 million part-time.
U.S. Census Bureau, Vintage 2025 estimates: U.S. resident population about 341.8 million on July 1, 2025.
Recruiting math (computed): if each person recruits 5, level n needs 5^n people; 5^13 = 1,220,703,125 > 341.8 million (U.S. population).
Buyback math (computed, illustrative): 90% x $1,050 = $945; Dave's damage $499 + $900 + $250 = $1,649; $1,649 - $945 - $240 = $464.

beats.text: Dave's garage is full of boxes. Forty boxes of protein shakes he can't sell.
Yep. That's Dave. How did he get here? Let's rewind.
Six months ago, his neighbor Bob said: it's not a party. It's a business opportunity.
Bob skipped one thing. In a big survey, nearly half the people who joined lost money.
So where does all that money go? Somebody gets it.
By the end, you'll know who. And the one sentence that got Dave his money back.
So Dave went to Bob's living room. Chips, folding chairs, and a slide with one big triangle.
Is that a pyramid, Dave asked? No, Bob said. It's a triangle of success.
Here's the deal. Dave can earn two ways. One, sell miracle shakes. Two, recruit friends to sell them, and get a cut of everything they buy.
Picture a lemonade stand where you earn more for signing up other kids than for selling lemonade.
To join, Dave needed a starter kit. Four hundred ninety nine dollars. Bob said it pays for itself in a month.
Dave signed up that night. But the kit was only the ticket in. The real cost had a cute name. Autoship.
So the first box arrived. A month later, another box arrived. Dave hadn't ordered it.
Bob explained. To stay active and earn commissions, Dave had to buy a minimum amount of product every month. One hundred fifty dollars. Automatically.
It's like paying your boss rent for your own desk, every month, just to keep your job.
Dave tried selling. His mom bought two boxes. A coworker bought one, to be nice. In six months, he sold two hundred forty dollars of shakes.
In the same six months, autoship took nine hundred dollars.
Dave was drinking shakes for breakfast, lunch and dinner. And Bob had a solution. Stop selling. Start recruiting.
So Dave bought a ticket to the big spring rally. Two hundred fifty dollars. Bright lights, loud music, and a man on stage holding a giant check.
The secret, the man said, is simple. Recruit five friends. Each of them recruits five. And so on.
Dave did the math on a napkin. Five people. Then twenty five. Then one hundred twenty five.
By level thirteen, you'd need more than one billion people. America has about three hundred forty two million.
It's a pizza that gets cut into more and more slices. The people who joined first got real slices. Everyone arriving now gets crumbs.
And that made Dave wonder. If the math runs out this fast, what do normal people actually earn?

Quick guess. One of the biggest companies in this industry has about one hundred eight thousand people reselling its products in America. In a typical month, how many earn anything at all? Write your guess in the comments. The answer is in a minute.
So Dave flipped a shake box over. On the back, a nutrition label. Calories, sugar, protein. The boring truth, in tiny print.
Turns out the business has a label too. It's called an income disclosure statement. Many big companies publish one. Bob had never shown it to him.
Dave found the twenty twenty five statement from Herbalife, one of the biggest names in the industry.
About one hundred eight thousand American distributors bought products to resell. In a typical month, about forty seven thousand earned any money at all.
Remember your guess? Fewer than half. And for first year sellers who did earn something, half made less than one hundred sixty six dollars that month. Before expenses.
Before shakes, gas and rally tickets. Dave's autoship alone was one hundred fifty.
So where was all that money going? Dave grabbed a marker, and followed it.
Dave drew the arrows. His one hundred fifty dollars a month went to the company. Then the company paid a slice of it up the line.
A slice to Bob. A slice to the woman who recruited Bob. A slice to the person above her. All the way to the top.
Wait. Bob earned money on Dave's autoship? Dave wasn't Bob's business partner. Dave was Bob's customer.
It's a staircase with a tiny toll booth on every step. And our old friend the raccoon is collecting at each one.
And at the very top? In that same statement, the top one percent of experienced sellers earned more than twenty one thousand dollars a month. Most had been in it five to twelve years.
So that's the villain. Not Bob. A pay plan where the money flows up, from the many at the bottom to the few at the top.
But if the money flows up like that, how is this even legal?
Dave thought: if this were a scam, it would be illegal. Nope. It's more complicated.
The F T C says a multi level marketing company can be legal, if people earn mainly by selling to real customers outside the business.
If they earn mainly from recruiting, or by buying stuff just to stay active, that starts to look like an illegal pyramid scheme.
Think of a bakery. A real bakery makes money when strangers buy bread. If its main customers are its own bakers, the bread isn't the business. The bakers are.

In twenty sixteen, the F T C charged Herbalife with misleading people about how much they could earn. Herbalife settled. It paid two hundred million dollars, and checks went to nearly three hundred fifty thousand people.
The deal also said at least two thirds of its rewards had to be based on real retail sales. So legal can be a line the government draws later.
And even when it's legal, the F T C's own advice page says most people who join make little or no money. Some lose money.
Dave read that twice. Then he looked at his phone, and realized he'd almost done something terrible.
On his screen was a message. To Grandma. Hey hun! I have an exciting opportunity for you.
Dave had become Bob. It's like a zombie movie. One bite, and suddenly you're chasing your own family.
And it's not rare. In that A A R P survey, about a third of people were recruited by a friend. About one in eight, by family.
Four in ten said the company misled them about their chances. And thirty nine percent quit because pitching friends and family felt so uncomfortable.
Dave called Bob. Bob went quiet. Then he admitted it. After the rallies and his own autoship, Bob was losing money too.
So Dave was down one thousand six hundred forty nine dollars, with forty boxes in the garage, and a text to Grandma he almost sent.
Dave deleted the message. Then he found one rule in the fine print that the upline never mentions.
This is education, not advice. Step one. Dave cancelled autoship, in writing, and saved the confirmation. Next month's charge: zero.
Step two. The rule. Companies in the Direct Selling Association promise to buy back sellable inventory you bought in the last twelve months, for at least ninety percent of what you paid.
It's like finding the receipt for a sweater you never wore.
Dave checked. Bob's company was a member. He counted his unopened boxes. One thousand fifty dollars of shakes, all bought this year.

Step three, for next time. Before joining anything, Dave asks for the income disclosure statement, and two questions from the F T C. What do people earn after expenses? And how much comes from customers outside the business?
If nobody can answer, that is the answer.
Then Dave called the company, and said one sentence. I'm cancelling, and I'd like the inventory buyback on my unopened products.

Three weeks later, nine hundred forty five dollars landed back in his account. Add the two hundred forty he sold, and his damage shrank from one thousand six hundred forty nine dollars to four hundred sixty four.
And the answer to the big question? The money went up the triangle. To the company, and the few at the top. Dave just stopped climbing.
One. Read the label first: the income disclosure.
Two. If you must buy every month to stay in, you're the customer.
Three. Leaving? Ask for the buyback. Ninety percent beats zero.
Next time, Dave downloads a game that's totally free. Three months later, his bank statement disagrees.
Subscribe. It's free, and unlike Bob's shakes, there's no autoship.

youtube.hook: Dave joined his neighbor's 'business opportunity.' Six months later: $1,649 spent, $240 earned, 40 boxes in the garage. Where did the money go? Most people who join multi-level marketing businesses lose money, but the industry keeps growing. Dave learns the hard way where his $1,649 actually went, who profits from 'business opportunities,' and the two questions that reveal the truth before you sign up. Plus: the one sentence that got him most of his money back.
